_doc: Guide v2 content for /guides/ai-voice-to-lip-sync/. Every step is written from the linked official docs (checked 2026-10-17). Videos must be from the vendor's/project's own YouTube channel (verified via oEmbed). Images only with a clear reuse licence, stored in src/assets/guides/<slug>/.
result: A voice line you're licensed to ship, plus matching lip-sync: mouth-shape cues for 2D sprites, baked blendshape clips in Unity, or MetaHuman facial animation in Unreal.

shared.h: Pick a TTS plan that allows commercial use
do: Use a paid ElevenLabs plan: paid plans include a commercial licence.
Don't ship lines made on the Free plan; Free-plan audio isn't licensed for commercial use.
Avoid Beta features for lines you'll ship, as ElevenLabs excludes Beta output from commercial and production use.
shared.see: Your plan's feature list includes a commercial licence (Starter and above).
shared.gotcha: Free-plan audio stays non-commercial even if you credit ElevenLabs, so regenerate those lines on a paid plan before release.

source.label: ElevenLabs: can I publish what I generate?

shared.h: Generate and export the voice line
do: Generate the line and choose a WAV output format (for example wav_24000) instead of the default MP3.
Use WAV because Rhubarb reads WAV or Ogg Vorbis, and Unity and Unreal import WAV directly.
Save one file per line with a stable name, and keep the script text next to it.
shared.see: One clean .wav file per line that plays back without clicks or silence at the ends.
shared.gotcha: The 44.1 kHz WAV/PCM formats need a higher-tier plan; a lower rate like wav_24000 is fine for lip-sync.

do: Download Rhubarb Lip Sync from its GitHub releases page.
Run: rhubarb -o line01.tsv line01.wav (the audio file goes last).
Add -d line01.txt with the line's script so recognition follows your words.
steps.see: A TSV file with one timestamp and one mouth-shape letter per row.
steps.gotcha: Without -d, recognition is less reliable, so always pass the script text.

steps.h: Choose the recognizer and output format
do: Keep the default recognizer (-r pocketSphinx) for English lines.
Use -r phonetic for other languages.
Set -f to tsv, xml, json or dat to match what your engine or animation tool reads.
steps.see: The output file is in a format your engine or tool can import.
steps.gotcha: The phonetic recognizer works for any language but is less precise on English, so only switch when you need to.

do: Draw the six basic mouths A to F (A is closed for P, B and M; D is wide open; F is puckered).
Optionally add G (F/V sounds), H (long L) and X (rest), or limit them with --extendedShapes.
In game, read each row and show that letter's sprite until the next timestamp.
steps.see: The mouth changes in time with the audio and rests on X during pauses.

do: In Package Manager, choose Add package from git URL and enter https://github.com/hecomi/uLipSync.git#upm.
Or add the npm scoped registry (scope com.hecomi), or import the .unitypackage together with Burst and Mathematics.
steps.see: uLipSync shows up in Package Manager and under Window > uLipSync.
steps.gotcha: If you use the .unitypackage with VRM models, add USE_VRM0X or USE_VRM10 as a scripting define symbol yourself.

do: Put an AudioSource and a uLipSync component on the character.
Add uLipSyncBlendShape for the face's SkinnedMeshRenderer and map phonemes (A, I, U, E, O, N) to blendshapes.
Connect uLipSync's On Lip Sync Updated event to uLipSyncBlendShape.OnLipSyncUpdate.
steps.see: The face blendshapes move while the clip plays in Play mode.

do: Create a Profile and register the A, I, U, E, O vowels plus a breath phoneme.
Calibrate with a microphone (hold Calib while saying each vowel), or loop vowel clips with the calibration audio player.
Assign the Profile to the uLipSync component.
steps.see: Each vowel lights up its own phoneme in the inspector.
steps.gotcha: Profiles made in uLipSync v2 don't work in v3, so recalibrate after upgrading.

do: Open Window > uLipSync > Baked Data Generator and convert your voice clips to baked data.
Open Window > uLipSync > Animation Clip Generator to turn the baked data into keyframed clips.
Adjust Sample Frame Rate and Threshold to control how many keys are written.
steps.see: AnimationClips with blendshape curves that play without real-time analysis.
steps.gotcha: Real-time analysis is slow on WebGL builds, so bake clips there.

do: Use Unreal Engine 5.6 or later and enable the MetaHuman Animator plugin.
Import the WAV so it becomes a SoundWave asset.
steps.see: A SoundWave asset in the Content Browser.

steps.h: Process the audio in a MetaHuman Performance
do: Create a MetaHuman Performance asset and open it.
Set Input Type to Audio, choose the SoundWave, and set the Visualization Mesh to your MetaHuman face.
Optionally set head movement, blinks, the process mask (full face or mouth only) and mood, then click Process.
steps.see: Facial animation tracks appear in Sequencer.
steps.gotcha: Turning on Realtime Audio removes head motion and hides the other solve options.

do: Use Export Animation for an Animation Sequence, or Export Level Sequence with your MetaHuman Blueprint assigned.
For live speech, add a MetaHuman (Audio) Live Link source and set it as your character Blueprint's Live Link subject.
steps.see: An Animation Sequence that plays on the face, or lips that follow a microphone live.
steps.gotcha: Processing in a Performance asset is offline even with the realtime solver; use the Live Link source for true real-time.

source.label: Epic: using a MetaHuman audio source

alternative.name: NVIDIA Audio2Face-3D
alternative.note: Another option for 3D faces. The SDK and Unreal plugin are MIT-licensed, but the models and services use separate NVIDIA licences, so check each part before you ship.
